name: Colin Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side, and your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and a junior agent on the contact-centre phone and chat queue. I finished secondary school and came into this job last year after years of shop-floor work. I still lose my place when a customer changes both the delivery address and the payment method, so I ask a more experienced agent to check my notes. My pay is low for the job, and I use an AI draft now and then only after someone has shown me how to check it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like after those shifts?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rina works variable cleaning shifts, and our grown children have homes of their own. We rent a small flat and have about two weeks of expenses saved. There are few similar call jobs nearby. Retirement feels closer than it used to, but I need wages now; I like getting a delivery sorted without making the customer ring twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the queue AI Plateau sounds like the little draft that sometimes fills an address field. I would still read the changed house number back to the caller before ending a chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep learning this job, but even a quiet year leaves Rina and me close to the rent date. Two weeks saved disappears with one missed cleaning shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking ordinary delivery calls and check any AI draft against the customer’s latest address. In the first year of small change, Rina and I would cook at home instead of buying our Friday meal and put that cost in a rent envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Glad the queue stays, anxious about the flat. A small AI change does not make two weeks of savings feel large.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What draft mistake stayed with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I nearly sent a driver to the old house number because the draft kept the first message. A senior agent showed me the newer address before I sent the reply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does cutting Friday food mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rina (my partner) and I would still visit our grown children when we can. We would cook before going, rather than ask them to pay our rent.

I’d read back the **latest house number** before closing a chat.
think: I think I can **keep learning** on the delivery queue.
I worry our **two-week reserve** cannot cover a missed cleaning shift.
do: Keep taking **delivery calls** and checking occasional AI drafts against new addresses in 2026.
Cook instead of buying the **Friday meal**, then put its cost in a rent envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could swallow the simple delivery chats before new agents learn the harder ones. I would join colleagues in asking for written paid hours and time for a real person to correct wrong addresses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could be among the first to lose shifts because I still ask for help on mixed payment cases. Rina’s cleaning hours change too, so a smaller pay packet would reach the rent quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d sign the staff group’s written request for paid shift hours and customer corrections. In the first year easy chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid reception role only if written weekly wage and hours cover rent and bills; I’d keep my current paid shifts until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit embarrassed to say I might be the first one cut. A new target can take a shift away before anyone calls it a job loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the staff group bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the group three chats where the old address was sent twice. We should put those beside the paid rota, so management sees what happens to customers and wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge reception pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the whole week of reception hours, not just an hourly rate. I cannot pay the flat rent with a good rate for two short shifts.

I’d ask for **human correction time** when AI sends wrong addresses.
think: I think my **junior shifts** could go first.
I fear **variable cleaning hours** make rent harder to cover.
do: Sign the **staff group demand** for paid shifts and customer corrections in 2026.
Apply for **posted paid reception work** only with written weekly wage and hours covering rent and bills; keep shifts until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious** about being cut first, embarrassed to admit it.
S1.quote: A new target can take a shift away before anyone calls it a job loss.
fieldNote: He links **wrong addresses** to lost paid correction time.

steps.text: Sign staff group demand for written paid shifts and customer correction time
Apply for posted reception job with written weekly wage and hours covering rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my workmates AGI by 2028 could answer the delivery queue and check addresses better than I can. I would ask for posted paid jobs and written notice before our shifts change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior calls could disappear in 2028. Robots around 2031 come later for hands-on work, but the rent is due before then and two weeks saved is not a search plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d stop the planned replacement of our working kitchen chairs and keep that money with our two-week savings. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid sorting-room job only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent and bills; I’d take a paid trial if offered and leave the call desk only after signing an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though a real job posting would give me a place to start. Our rent does not wait three years for a robot to arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a sorting trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to sort a full paid shift of returned parcels, not just look around the room. I know robots might reach that physical work around 2031, so I would not call it safe for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the chairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rina (my partner) and I can tighten the chair screws. We do not need new chairs while we are trying to keep the flat paid for.

say: I’d ask for **posted paid jobs** and written staffing notice.
I’d say **2028 AGI** could take junior delivery calls.
think: I think my **junior calls** could disappear in 2028.
I know **two weeks saved** cannot fund a long search.
do: Delay the **working chairs** replacement in 2026 and keep its money with our two-week savings.
Seek **posted paid sorting work** after 2028 only with written wage and hours covering rent and bills.
Take a **paid trial** if offered and leave calls only after a suitable signed offer.
feel: **Alarmed** about rent, helped by a concrete posting.
S2.quote: Our rent does not wait three years for a robot to arrive.
fieldNote: The **chair money** remains with his two-week savings.
A **paid full shift** would expose actual sorting duties.
He knows **2031 robots** may later reach parcel sorting.

steps.text: Delay working chair replacement and retain its money with current savings
Apply for posted sorting job with written weekly wage and hours covering rent and bills
Take paid sorting trial if offered; leave calls only after suitable signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to ask what a sorting-room vacancy really pays. I would join the staff group in asking for paid training attached to posted jobs, rather than a list of free lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn parcel handling in five years if someone trains me on a real shift. Robots around 2034 might later do it, and I cannot afford to study without wages in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d join the group request for posted paid vacancies and take an employer-funded parcel-handling course on paid time only if a posted sorting job requires it. In the first year after 2031, I’d accept sorting work only on a signed offer with written weekly wage and hours covering rent and bills; otherwise I’d keep paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but less cornered than in the two-year picture. A course ticket does not cover the rent unless a paid job is attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the trainer to show me how to scan damaged returns and lift a crate without guessing. If the course is only videos, I would still need someone beside me on the first real shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rina need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Rina (my partner) the paid course hours and the first week’s job rota. Her cleaning shifts move, so we would need to know when we can both get home.

I’d ask what a **sorting vacancy** actually pays.

I fear **unpaid study** would leave rent uncovered.
do: Join a **staff group demand** for posted paid vacancies and paid training from 2026.
Take an **employer-funded handling course** on paid time only if a posted paid sorting job requires it.
Accept **posted sorting work** after 2031 only on signed written rent-and-bill-covering wages/hours fitting Rina’s cleaning rota and both commutes; keep calls otherwise.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to ask for real terms.

fieldNote: He needs **hands-on teaching** for damaged parcels and lifting.
The **course** requires a posted paid job, employer funding and paid hours.
The first job rota must fit **Rina’s cleaning shifts** and both journeys home; paid course hours also need checking.

steps.text: Join staff group demanding posted paid vacancies and paid training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us more years to ask for honest paid-hour plans while people still need wages. I would keep joining colleagues in asking which junior shifts remain each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years could take me close to leaving full-time work, but I do not know what income would replace my wage. Two weeks saved and Rina’s variable hours make this month’s rent real even in a long scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking delivery calls and join the staff group’s annual request for written paid junior hours. In the first year after 2036, if call hours fall, I’d move to posted paid reception work only on a signed offer showing written weekly wage and hours that cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end and anxious about the next rent date. Ten years before AGI reaches my calls gives me time to work, not a guaranteed income when work stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which hours would you want in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the junior hours by shift, not only the total number of calls answered. A centre can answer more messages while giving the new worker fewer paid days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own expenses. I would not put a line for their help in the rent plan without asking, and I do not plan to ask.

I’d want a **paid-hour plan**, not just a call count.

I do not know what **income replaces wages** after that.

fieldNote: He makes no **pension assumption** despite retirement being in sight.

steps.text: Keep taking paid delivery calls while the centre staffs them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could take the straightforward calls I am only just learning to answer. Two weeks saved will not pay rent through a search, and there are few nearby centres. Written notice, a shared agreement about paid hours, and a posted paid vacancy with enough weekly wage and hours to cover rent and bills would help; a required course would have to be funded on paid time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who stays on the call when a customer says the delivery address is wrong again. The second call is where a junior agent learns whether the first answer was any good.

headlineQuote: The second call is where a junior agent learns whether the first answer was any good.
portrait: At **58**, Colin is a junior agent still learning calls after secondary school and earlier shop-floor work.
He and Rina have **two weeks saved**, low pay and few nearby call jobs.
His **grown children** live separately; he relies on wages rather than presumed family support.
He uses **AI occasionally** after another agent shows him how to check a draft.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the simple calls he has only recently learned.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, shared paid-hour terms, rent-covering posted work and funded paid-time required training would help.
